title: a table, bread, wine, remember me
hook: a table, bread, wine, remember me

segments.voice: Yesterday, silence. Not the wind, not the earthquake, not the fire. A still small voice. Your line: quiet is where he is. Did you find your one quiet minute? Day nineteen.

Think of a meal you'll never forget. Maybe a holiday table. Maybe the last dinner with someone before they moved away, or before they died. You probably don't remember what you ate. You remember who was there, and what somebody said. Now picture an upstairs room in Jerusalem, at Passover. Thirteen men around a table. One of them already knows he's going to be betrayed, and that he won't live to see the weekend out. And instead of a speech, he picks up the bread. That's the last supper. And the thing he did with the bread and the cup, Christians have done every week, somewhere on earth, for two thousand years. Today's word is that meal.
screen: `A MEAL YOU'LL NEVER FORGET.` → `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM. PASSOVER.` → `HE PICKS UP THE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Communion. Here's a surprise first: the oldest written account of that night isn't in the Gospels. It's in a letter. Paul wrote to the church in Corinth about twenty years later, and passed on what he'd been taught. In the old King James Bible: "the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." Then the cup, and the same words again: in remembrance of me. The Greek word for remembrance is anamnesis. It's more than a memory you have in your head. It's a remembering you do, with your hands, so the thing is present again. Families do this at every holiday table. Jews do it at Passover, telling the story as if they'd been there. That was the meal Jesus was eating. The meal has several names. Communion, from a word Paul uses for sharing: all of us, one loaf. The Eucharist, from the Greek for giving thanks, because that's what he did first. The Lord's Supper. The Mass. And here's where Christians honestly differ, so here's who says what. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe Christ is truly present in the bread and the wine. Not a symbol. Him. Many Protestants understand the meal as a memorial: the bread and wine are signs, and the remembering is the heart of it. And many others, Lutherans and Anglicans and more, stand somewhere in between, with their own careful words for it. Churches have argued about this for centuries, and they still do. What they all do is the same thing: a table, bread, a cup, and the words, remember me.
screen: `THE OLDEST ACCOUNT IS A LETTER.` · `ANAMNESIS — REMEMBERING YOU DO.` · `COMMUNION. EUCHARIST. THE MASS.` · `WHO BELIEVES WHAT.` · then, large: `A MEAL IS A MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a table from your life, with people around it. Maybe it's this week's. Maybe it's one from long ago. Picture who was there. Picture their hands, passing something. Hear one thing somebody said. Let yourself remember them, not just think about them. If you pray, you can hold those people in your prayer, the way this meal holds someone. If you don't, just let the table be full again for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Communion. Sharing one loaf and one cup. A meal that is a memory. Nineteenth word.
Your line: a meal is a memory. Today, eat one meal slowly. And if you're eating with someone, put your phone away and remember that this one counts too. Day nineteen.

howItsDone: Christians share communion with bread and wine (or grape juice) as Jesus did at the last supper. Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate it at every Mass or Divine Liturgy; many Protestant churches share it weekly, monthly or a few times a year.

fork.setup: it's the night you know you'll be betrayed. thirteen friends around one table at Passover. what do you do?
options: give a long farewell speech about what to believe.
take bread, give thanks, break it, and say: remember me.
leave the city before anyone comes.
fork.reveal: he took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said "this do in remembrance of me." not a lecture: a meal, to be done again and again.

original.note: Greek. remembrance, remembering. "this do in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24).

trapdoor: what you thought: a small bit of bread and a sip in church.
what it means: the meal Jesus gave on the night he was betrayed, which Christians repeat, remembering him.
what a scholar hears: Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11, written about twenty years after, is older than any Gospel. and anamnesis is a remembering you act out, not just recall.

notes: Beliefs about the Eucharist are summarized briefly (Catholic and Orthodox: real presence; many Protestants: memorial; Lutherans, Anglicans and others in between). Reformed Christians (e.g. Calvin's spiritual presence) are folded into 'many others'. Please check each group would recognize itself; the memorial wording especially.
1 Corinthians dated about twenty years after the crucifixion (c. AD 53–55) and before the Gospels: the common scholarly view; confirm wording.
'Communion' from Paul's word koinonia (1 Cor 10:16, 'the communion of the body of Christ'): stated as 'a word Paul uses for sharing'.
John's Gospel sets the supper just before Passover; the Synoptics make it a Passover meal. The script follows the Synoptic setting ('at Passover'); a Keeper may want a hedge.
Grape juice mentioned in howItsDone for churches that use it.
